subject: astronaut sleeping
title: What If You Fell Asleep in Space?

scenes.text: What if you fell asleep in space? Your own breath could become the problem.
You zip into a sleeping bag tied to a wall. Outside, 16 sunrises pass every 24 hours.
On Earth, warm breath rises away from your face. Weightless, it just hangs there all night.
Hours in, exhaled carbon dioxide can build a bubble around your head, leaving you short of air.
So every bunk sits near a fan. Crews get eight and a half hours for sleep, yet 85 astronauts averaged about six.
The irony? Space is silent, but the fans keeping you alive are so loud astronauts sleep in earplugs.

description:
What if you fell asleep in space? In weightlessness warm exhaled air does not rise, so without ventilation a bubble of carbon dioxide can form around a sleeper's head, which is why ISS crews sleep near a fan, in sleeping bags fixed to a wall, with 16 sunrises every 24 hours.
A Harvard and Brigham and Women's study of 85 astronauts found they averaged about six hours of sleep against 8.5 scheduled, and most used sleep medication. Station noise means earplugs and eye masks are standard.
